lessons.title: Lesson 1: Setting up to type safely
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set up your chair, keyboard and screen and sit in a posture that does not strain your body.
This lesson builds toward: Given a chair, a desk and a computer, you will set up the chair, keyboard and screen and sit in a safe typing posture, meeting at least 5 of the 6 points on the set-up checklist.
Typing for hours in a bad position can cause pain in your neck, back, wrists and hands. A good set-up costs nothing and helps you type faster, because relaxed hands move more easily.
OSHA, the US workplace safety agency, describes a neutral posture for computer work: head and neck balanced in line with your body, shoulders relaxed, elbows close to your body, wrists and hands straight in line with your forearms, lower back supported and feet flat on the floor. The top of the screen should be at or just below eye level. There is no one perfect position for everyone, so adjust until it feels easy.
Keep the keyboard close, so you do not reach. Let your fingers float over the keys and tap them lightly; do not rest your wrists hard on the desk edge while typing. Take short breaks to stand, stretch and look away from the screen. If typing ever causes pain, tingling or numbness that does not go away, stop and talk to a doctor or nurse.
Step by step:
- Sit back in the chair so your lower back is supported. Use a rolled towel or cushion if needed.
- Put your feet flat on the floor or on a box or footrest.
- Pull the keyboard close so your elbows stay near your sides.
- Keep your wrists straight, in line with your forearms, and your shoulders relaxed.
- Move the screen so the top is at or just below eye level.
- Plan a short break to stand and stretch about every 30 to 60 minutes.
Words to know:
- Posture: the way you hold your body when you sit or stand.
- Neutral posture: a relaxed, balanced position where your joints are not bent or twisted.
- Ergonomics: setting up work and tools so they fit your body and do not hurt it.
- OSHA: the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, the US agency for workplace safety.
Official sources:
- OSHA: Computer Workstations eTool
Try it now: Copy this six-point checklist on paper: back supported, feet flat, elbows close, wrists straight, shoulders relaxed, screen top at or below eye level. Sit at the computer you will practice on, tick each point you meet, and fix any you do not.
You can now set up a chair, keyboard and screen for safe typing and check your posture with a six-point checklist.

check.q: Where should the top of your computer screen be?
options: At or just below eye level
check.why: OSHA's guidance puts the top of the monitor at or just below eye level so your neck stays balanced.

check.q: Your wrists bend up sharply while you type. What do you change?
options: Adjust the chair or keyboard so your wrists are straight
check.why: Wrists should be straight, in line with your forearms; bent wrists add strain.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: The home row and the finger map
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Place your fingers on the home row and press each letter key with the right finger without looking.
This lesson builds toward: Using a computer keyboard, you will place your fingers on the home row and press each letter key with the correct finger, typing a full line of drill without looking at the keys.
Touch typing means typing without looking at the keys. Each finger has its own keys, so your hands learn where the letters are. It feels slower at first, but after a few weeks of practice it becomes faster and more accurate than looking.
Your fingers start and return to the home row. Left hand: little finger on A, ring finger on S, middle finger on D, pointer on F. Right hand: pointer on J, middle on K, ring on L, little finger on the semicolon (;). Your thumbs rest on the space bar. Most keyboards have a small bump on F and J so you can find home without looking.
Each finger reaches up and down from its home key. Left pinky: Q, A, Z. Left ring: W, S, X. Left middle: E, D, C. Left pointer: R, F, V and also T, G, B. Right pointer: Y, H, N and also U, J, M. Right middle: I, K and the comma. Right ring: O, L and the period. Right pinky: P, the semicolon, the slash and the Enter key. After each reach, the finger goes back home.
Step by step:
- Find the bumps on F and J with your pointer fingers.
- Rest the other fingers on A S D and K L ;, thumbs on the space bar.
- Look at the screen, not your hands. Cover your hands with a cloth if you keep looking.
- Type slowly: reach with the correct finger, then return it home.
- Say each letter quietly as you type it at first, and keep a steady rhythm.
Words to know:
- Touch typing: typing without looking at the keys, using the same finger for each key every time.
- Home row: the middle row of letters where your fingers rest: A S D F and J K L ;.
- Hunt and peck: looking for each key and pressing it with one or two fingers.
- Reach: moving a finger from its home key to another key and back.
Try it now: Open Notepad, TextEdit, Google Docs or Word. Without looking at your hands, type each line three times: asdf jkl; then fdsa ;lkj then sad lad fall flask then dad has a glass. Then type: the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog. Count how many times you looked down.
You can now find the home row by feel, use the right finger for each letter, and practice a line without looking at the keys.

check.q: Which keys have small bumps to help you find the home row?
check.why: The bumps on F and J let your pointer fingers find home without looking.

check.q: Which finger types the letter E?
check.why: E is the reach up from D, which belongs to the left middle finger.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Capitals, numbers, symbols and the number pad
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Type capital letters, numbers and common symbols, and enter numbers on the number pad.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of phone numbers, prices, dates and capitals, you will type numbers, symbols and capital letters with the number row, the Shift keys and the number pad, with no more than 2 mistakes in 10 lines.
For a capital letter, hold the Shift key with the little finger of the OTHER hand, press the letter, then let go. For a capital A (left hand), use the right Shift. For a capital J (right hand), use the left Shift. Caps Lock is for typing a whole word in capitals; turn it off after.
The number row is above the letters. Each finger reaches up from its home key: left pinky types 1, left ring 2, left middle 3, left pointer 4 and 5, right pointer 6 and 7, right middle 8, right ring 9, right pinky 0. Symbols on the same keys, such as $ % @ # and !, need Shift.
Many desktop keyboards have a number pad on the right, laid out like a calculator. Data entry, billing, banking and stock jobs use it a lot. Turn on Num Lock. Rest the right pointer on 4, middle finger on 5 (it has a bump) and ring finger on 6. The thumb presses 0 and the little finger presses Enter. Many laptops have no number pad; then use the number row.
Step by step:
- Capitals: hold Shift with the opposite hand's little finger, press the letter, let go.
- Number row: reach up from home with the same finger, then come back.
- Symbols: hold Shift and press the number key that shows the symbol.
- Number pad: turn on Num Lock and rest on 4 5 6, using the bump on 5.
- Check numbers twice; one wrong digit in a price or phone number is a real error.
Words to know:
- Shift key: the key you hold down to get a capital letter or the top symbol on a key.
- Caps Lock: a key that makes every letter a capital until you press it again.
- Number pad: the block of number keys on the right side of many keyboards, also called the numeric keypad or 10-key.
- Num Lock: the key that turns the number pad's numbers on.
- Data entry: typing information such as names, numbers and codes into a computer system.
Try it now: Type these ten lines, then check each one against the page: (555) 014-2290 | $12.75 | 03/15/2026 | Order #4471 | 40% off | Maria Lopez | Dr. Kim, Room 210 | 7:30 a.m. | ID 88-31-05 | Total: $1,049.60. Use the number pad if you have one. Count your mistakes and practice the lines you missed.
You can now type capitals with the opposite Shift key, enter numbers and symbols from the number row, and use the number pad from 4 5 6.

check.q: You want a capital P (a right-hand key). Which Shift do you hold?
options: Either Shift with the same hand
check.why: Use the Shift on the opposite hand, so the right hand is free to press P.

check.q: On the number pad, where does your middle finger rest?
options: On 5, the key with the bump
check.why: The number pad home keys are 4 5 6, and 5 has the bump for your middle finger.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Speed, accuracy and a plan

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Measuring your speed and accuracy
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate your words per minute and accuracy from a timed typing test.
This lesson builds toward: Given a one-minute or longer timed typing test, you will calculate your words per minute and your accuracy, with both numbers worked out correctly.
Typing speed is counted in words per minute (WPM). Because words have different lengths, typing tests count every 5 characters (letters, spaces and punctuation) as one word. So if you type 200 characters in one minute, that is 200 divided by 5 = 40 WPM. For a longer test, divide by the minutes too: 450 characters in 3 minutes is 90 words divided by 3 = 30 WPM.
Accuracy tells you how many of your words were right. Accuracy = correct words divided by all words typed, times 100. If you typed 50 words and 4 had mistakes, accuracy is 46 divided by 50 = 92%. Some tests also give net WPM, which takes off for mistakes: errors divided by minutes, subtracted from your speed.
Accuracy matters more than speed. A fast typist who makes many mistakes is slow at work, because every mistake must be found and fixed. Build accuracy first, then speed. You can time yourself with a phone timer and a text editor (many programs show a character count), or use a free practice site such as typing.com, which shows speed and accuracy for you.
Step by step:
- Choose a paragraph you have not practiced, from a book, a news story or a job post.
- Set a timer for 1 minute (or 3 minutes for a steadier score).
- Type at your normal pace without stopping to fix mistakes.
- Count the characters, including spaces, or use the program's character count.
- Speed: characters divided by 5, then divided by the minutes.
- Accuracy: correct words divided by words typed, times 100. Write both down with the date.
Words to know:
- WPM: words per minute: how many words you type in one minute.
- Standard word: 5 characters, including spaces and punctuation, counted as one word in typing tests.
- Accuracy: the percent of what you typed that is correct.
- Net WPM: your speed after taking off for mistakes.
- Character: any letter, number, space or symbol you type.
Official sources:
- Typing.com (free typing lessons and tests)
Try it now: Take a one-minute test: set a timer, type a new paragraph from a job post or news story, and stop when the timer ends. Count the characters (or use the character count), work out your WPM, mark your mistakes, and work out your accuracy. Write both numbers and today's date at the top of a page. This is your starting score.
You can now time yourself, work out your words per minute and your accuracy, and record a starting score.

check.q: You typed 250 characters in one minute. What is your speed?
check.why: 250 characters divided by 5 is 50 words, in one minute: 50 WPM.

check.q: You typed 40 words and 2 had mistakes. What is your accuracy?
check.why: 38 correct divided by 40 typed is 0.95, which is 95%.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Shortcuts and editing keys that save time
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use keyboard shortcuts to select, copy, paste, undo and save without the mouse.
This lesson builds toward: While typing and fixing a short document, you will use keyboard shortcuts to select, copy, paste, undo and save, doing all five without the mouse.
Every time you reach for the mouse, your hands leave the home row. Keyboard shortcuts let you edit without stopping. On Windows they use the Ctrl key; on a Mac most use the Command key instead.
The core five: Ctrl+A selects all, Ctrl+C copies, Ctrl+V pastes, Ctrl+Z undoes your last change, and Ctrl+S saves. Ctrl+X cuts (removes and copies). To do a shortcut, hold Ctrl down, tap the letter, then let go of both.
Editing keys help too. Backspace deletes to the left of the cursor; Delete removes to the right. The arrow keys move the cursor. Home and End jump to the start or end of a line. Hold Shift with an arrow key to select text a letter at a time. In many programs, Ctrl with the left or right arrow jumps a whole word. Fix a mistake when you see it, but do not stop typing to look back at every letter.
Step by step:
- Hold Ctrl (Command on a Mac) with your left little finger.
- Tap the letter: A select all, C copy, X cut, V paste, Z undo, S save.
- Let go of both keys.
- Use Shift with the arrow keys to select part of a line.
- Practice each shortcut five times so it becomes a habit.
Words to know:
- Shortcut: a key combination that does a task without the mouse.
- Ctrl: the Control key on a Windows keyboard, used for most shortcuts.
- Command key: the key with the symbol on Mac keyboards that does what Ctrl does on Windows.
- Cursor: the blinking line that shows where your typing will go.
- Undo: take back the last change you made.
Try it now: Type three short lines about a job you want. Then, without touching the mouse: select all (Ctrl+A), copy (Ctrl+C), click to the end with the End and arrow keys, paste (Ctrl+V), undo the paste (Ctrl+Z), and save the file (Ctrl+S). On a Mac, use Command in place of Ctrl. Do it twice.
You can now select, copy, cut, paste, undo and save with the keyboard and move around a line with the editing keys.

check.q: You just deleted a paragraph by accident. Which shortcut brings it back on Windows?
On a Mac, which key do most shortcuts use instead of Ctrl?
check.why: Most Mac shortcuts use the Command key where Windows uses Ctrl.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Your practice plan and the job typing test
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a four-week practice plan with your starting score, a goal, daily drills and a log.
This lesson builds toward: Using your own starting test score, you will write a four-week practice plan with a goal, daily drills, dates and a log, that meets every row of the course rubric. Given a one-minute or longer timed typing test, you will calculate your words per minute and your accuracy, with both numbers worked out correctly.
Typing improves with short daily practice, not long weekend sessions. 10 to 15 minutes a day, most days, works better than an hour once a week, because your fingers build habits through repetition. Keep your eyes on the screen and your posture neutral every time.
A good daily session has four parts: a 2-minute warm-up on the home row, a drill on your weakest keys (the ones you missed most in your test), a short drill on numbers or shortcuts, and real text such as a job post or a news story. Once a week, take a timed test and write the score in your log. Set a goal for accuracy first, then speed, and compare each week to your starting score.
Some employers give a typing test before hiring. The job post or the hiring office usually says what is tested and the speed they want; if it does not, ask. Before the test: sit in a good position, warm up for two minutes, read the instructions, and type steadily without rushing. Never pay a website that promises a typing certificate as a condition of getting a job; the employer gives its own test.
Step by step:
- Write your starting WPM, accuracy and the date from Lesson 4.
- Set a goal for week 4: accuracy first, then speed.
- List your weakest keys from your test.
- Plan each day: warm-up, weak-key drill, number or shortcut drill, real text.
- Pick one day a week for a timed test and make a log table: date, WPM, accuracy, note.
- Add a plan for test day: posture, warm-up, read the instructions, steady pace.
Words to know:
- Practice plan: a written schedule of what you will practice, when, and how you will measure progress.
- Log: a table where you write your scores each week.
- Weak keys: the keys you miss or slow down on most often.
- Pre-employment test: a test an employer gives to check a skill before hiring.
Official sources:
- Typing.com (free typing lessons and tests)
Try it now: Final task: write your four-week practice plan. Put your starting WPM and accuracy from Lesson 4 at the top, set a goal for each, list your weakest keys, and write each day's 10 to 15 minute session with dates. Add a log table with four weekly test rows and a short test-day plan.
You can now write and follow a four-week typing plan with a starting score, goals, daily drills and a weekly log, and prepare for a job typing test.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Starting score No starting score, or WPM and accuracy are worked out wrong. Starting WPM and accuracy from a timed test, worked out correctly, with the date. Also shows the working (characters, minutes, mistakes) so someone else can check it. Goals and dates No goal, or no dates for the four weeks. A goal for accuracy and for speed, with dates for each day or week. The goal is realistic for 10 to 15 minutes a day and has a checkpoint at week 2. Daily drills Practice is just "type more". Each session has a home-row warm-up, a drill on named weak keys and real text. Weak keys change week by week based on the log. Numbers and shortcuts No number, symbol or shortcut practice in the plan. The plan includes number or number-pad lines and the core shortcuts. The number practice matches a target job, such as prices for retail or IDs for data entry. Shortcut use Uses the mouse for every copy, paste, undo and save. Can show select all, copy, paste, undo and save with the keyboard. Also uses Home, End and Shift with the arrows to edit. Safe set-up and test day No posture check or test-day plan. The plan starts each session with the six-point set-up check and has a test-day plan. Includes planned breaks and what to do if typing hurts. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which practice schedule usually builds typing skill best?
options: Only practicing the night before a test
Practicing only when you feel like it
check.why: Short, regular practice builds finger habits through repetition.

check.q: What belongs at the top of your practice plan?
options: Your starting WPM, accuracy and the date
check.why: A starting score lets you set a goal and see your progress each week.
